name: Wendy Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did your morning involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy Gupta, fifty-eight, and I prepare dental-practice accounts and tax-return drafts at an accounting firm. This morning a patient deposit sat in the wrong month; I liked tracing it to the booking diary with the manager. I dislike a draft return sent before that call is made. I have a bachelor's degree in accounting and am still junior, with less skill than the senior reviewers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are your tools and home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I never use AI tools and keep the signed checklist beside my screen. My husband Ravi manages a hardware shop and our grown daughters live elsewhere; we paid off our home before they moved out. This firm pays its junior band well, we have eleven months of expenses saved and plenty of similar accounting firms nearby. I prefer a known process and a family budget built on actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still sort the dental practices' payment records and draft their accounts and tax returns for a senior to check. The appointment deposits do not always match the bank. A small sorting tool cannot ask which patient changed a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team to keep the original booking record beside the ledger. I'd tell the dentist that the firm signs the figures, not the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I never use AI tools; I like the checklist that the senior taught me. I'm fifty-eight and still junior, with a bachelor's degree in accounting, and I am slower than our strong reviewers. The practice pays its junior band well, and Ravi and I have eleven months saved with plenty of accounting firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drafting the dental accounts under senior review and ask the clinic for a corrected deposit list when numbers differ. I'd use our existing worksheet and keep the household budget and savings transfer as they are. I would not pay for a new tool that solves a small problem we already understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The work is familiar and our home bills have room around them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week one patient moved an appointment and the deposit landed in the wrong month. I called the manager and changed the entry only after she checked the booking diary. That careful call is why the dentist trusts us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did your household build room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi and I paid down our mortgage before our grown daughters moved out, and the house is ours now. He manages a small hardware shop on the high street. I like calling a practice manager to settle a deposit difference, and I dislike a draft return being sent as though a green tick were a signature.

say: I would keep **booking records** beside the ledger before the dental accounts are signed.
I would keep a **person signing** each tax return.
think: Our **eleven-month reserve** and owned home make present work and bills feel secure.
My **junior skill** still depends on senior checks.
do: Continue **dental accounts** with the familiar worksheet and senior sign-off.
Resolve **deposit differences** with practice managers before filing.
feel: I feel **calm** about present work and money.
S0.quote: A small sorting tool cannot ask which patient changed a booking.
fieldNote: The **high junior pay** comes from her firm’s pay band, not senior status or above-average accounting skill.
Her **owned home**, eleven-month reserve and many nearby firms support calm; she never uses AI tools.

steps.text: Keep drafting dental accounts under senior sign-off with existing worksheet
Ask clinic for corrected deposit list and resolve booking differences before filing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a system writes returns and answers routine questions, the partners may need fewer junior draft hours. I would want to know whether my own three-day rota remains paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written rota and a named person responsible for each dental return. I'd tell the partners that an account with a wrong deposit month is still wrong even when it was drafted quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose a paid day, and that would change our income even with savings. Ravi's hardware-shop wage and our eleven-month reserve give us time to compare jobs, but I do not want to use the reserve for ordinary bills. I won't start using AI simply because another person says it is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring six weeks of deposit corrections to the partner in January and ask which paid junior hours remain. I'd keep my current three days while the firm offers them. If my day is cut, I'd apply only to posted paid accounts roles with written pay covering our regular bills, a signed start and travel time fitting Ravi's confirmed shop hours; if no role fits, I'd keep any paid firm days offered and search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut to my own hours, but I have time to compare offers. A savings account is not a weekly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would another firm affect Wednesday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi closes the shop on Wednesday and I normally handle the evening meal then. A new firm's late close would mean we change that plan, but I want to see the actual hours first. We have no school pickups now; our daughters live elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the corrections show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The six-week list would show how many drafts still needed a call to the clinic manager. If the partners can fund those calls, I will do them. If not, I would rather hear that before our rota is changed.

say: I would request a **written paid rota** before any junior hours are cut.
I would keep **named responsibility** on dental returns.
think: My **three-day wage** could shrink if software replaces first drafts.
Our **reserve** gives search time, not a replacement payslip.
do: Show **six weeks of corrections** at January’s pay meeting.
Seek **posted paid work** after day cuts with written bill-covering pay, signed start and travel fitting Ravi’s confirmed shop hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours.
S1.quote: A savings account is not a weekly wage.
fieldNote: The **own-day risk** reaches her income despite high junior pay, a paid-off home and eleven months saved.
A **different accounting firm** must post a paid role with written bill-covering pay, signed start and compatible travel.

steps.text: Keep paid dental reviews and bring six-week correction list to January meeting
Seek posted paid work after cut with written bill-covering pay, signed start and Ravi-compatible travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 could prepare and check the dental accounts I draft. Robots come around 2031, but my work is at the desk and phone before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for a written end date and any paid patient-contact work they can fund. I'd tell Ravi we should keep the reserve for living expenses, not spend it on a new kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm might end my junior post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028. Eleven months saved and our owned home mean we can look carefully, though Ravi's shop wage alone would not cover every bill indefinitely. I do not know whether any pension is payable then; I will ask for a statement rather than assume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd defer the one-time eight-hundred kitchen cupboard order and hold the money in our reserve. While still employed, I'd check posted dental-clinic front-desk roles that include in-person patient help, though bookings and messages are thinking work AGI may also do. If my accounting post ends in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a funded clinic role with written bill-covering pay, a signed start and hours fitting Ravi's confirmed shop rota; if none fits, I'd keep any paid files the firm still offers and draw no more than our monthly budget cap from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a likely loss of my own wage, even with time to search. The reserve buys eleven months, not an eleven-year income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughters help financially?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi and I would tell our grown daughters we are pausing the cupboards, not asking them for money. I would write the monthly spending cap on the kitchen calendar. If the clinic has no funded opening, a friendly receptionist cannot put me on the payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a clinic desk any safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dental front desk may be automated too, so I would ask which tasks still need a person to welcome patients. I would not resign for an unposted role. A confirmed wage and start matter more than a conversation.

say: I would seek **written notice** and funded contact work.
I would preserve the **reserve for bills** rather than cupboards.
think: My **junior desk post** may end in the first year after 2028.
Our **eleven-month cushion** buys search time, not lifelong income.
do: Defer the **one-time cupboard order** and hold eight hundred.
Check **in-person clinic postings** while employed; retain only offered paid work and capped reserve spending if no role fits.
Take **funded clinic work** after 2028 loss only with written bill-covering pay, signed start and hours fitting Ravi’s confirmed shop rota.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely wage loss.
S2.quote: The reserve buys eleven months, not an eleven-year income.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches both her accountant desk and clinic booking work in 2028; later robots are irrelevant to most tasks.
The **clinic alternative** needs a posted funded vacancy, written bill-covering pay, signed start and Ravi-compatible hours; withdrawals stay capped.

steps.text: Defer one-time cupboard order and hold eight hundred in reserve
Check posted in-person clinic roles now; move after loss only for funded paid work
Accept only written bill-covering pay, signed start and hours fitting Ravi’s confirmed shop rota
Keep offered paid firm files and cap reserve withdrawals if no suitable clinic post

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let us check whether patient-facing work remains paid when AGI arrives in 2031. Robots around 2034 might change physical tasks, but the account and booking desks change first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to name funded work, and I'd ask local clinics to post actual paid roles. I'd tell colleagues not to call a friendly referral an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I could be near a pension date, but I have no statement showing an amount or start. Our home and savings give us time, not proof I can stop earning. I do not want my grown daughters to make up a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd request pension statements for Ravi and me, and compare the payable amounts and dates with our household bills. I'd keep my paid dental returns while offered and check posted clinic roles every two months. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my tax post ends and pension income is insufficient or not payable, I'd take a funded in-person clinic role only with written bill-covering pay, a signed start and hours fitting Ravi's confirmed shop rota; if no role fits, I'd keep offered paid firm hours and spend within our reserve cap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing paid work, though the longer runway and savings give us time. A pension date without an amount is an empty calendar square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a clinic manager hire you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call a clinic manager about a posted vacancy, not ask for a personal favour. If the work is only automated appointment messages, the role may not last. I would ask about the actual paid patient-contact hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pension statement decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi and I would look at our statements at the kitchen table. If they show enough payable income, we can decide separately whether to stop work; if not, we need an actual job. The daughters should not be our bridge.

I would ask for **funded patient contact** with stated hours.

S3.quote: A pension date without an amount is an empty calendar square.
fieldNote: Her **sixty-three-year age** does not establish pension entitlement or adequacy; the written statement determines whether work remains necessary.
The **clinic path** needs a posted funded role with real patient hours, written bill-covering pay, signed start and Ravi-compatible rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years would put me at sixty-eight, but I will not call that a funded retirement until we see the pension amounts. AGI in 2036 still reaches accounts and bookings before robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for dates and funded roles, and tell our daughters to build their own households. I'd tell clients a person should still be named when accounts are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our paid-off home and eleven months saved give us a choice if a pension covers the bills. I have not seen a payable figure yet, so I would not promise to leave work. A date on a form cannot pay the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check both pension statements and our bill budget each January while keeping paid returns if the firm offers them. I'd inspect posted local clinic roles yearly so I know the written wages and hours, without resigning for an invitation. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my tax post ends and pension income is inadequate or not payable, I'd take only a posted funded in-person clinic role with written bill-covering pay, signed start and hours fitting Ravi's confirmed shop rota; if none fits, I'd keep any paid firm files still offered and stay within our reserve budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because ten years and our owned home give room to choose. I still want the pension number in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would daughters help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi and I would not count our daughters' wages in the budget. If the pension covers everything at a real payment date, we may choose to stop then. If it does not, I will look for paid work with a signed start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start your own dental business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put savings into a new dental business just because the clinic knows me. A posted vacancy is a different matter. If the firm still pays me for file checks, I will keep those hours during the search.

I would keep **daughters’ wages** outside our budget.

S4.quote: A date on a form cannot pay the electricity bill.
fieldNote: At **sixty-eight in 2036**, retirement remains conditional on an actual payable pension covering household bills.
The **paid clinic fallback** requires a posted funded role, written bill-covering pay, signed start and shop-compatible hours; offered file checks continue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior dental-account drafts could disappear quickly. Our home and savings buy time, but Ravi's shop wage alone might not cover every bill. Written notice, a posted funded job and a signed start would help. A savings account is a cushion, not a payslip.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who phones the practice manager when a patient deposit is in the wrong month. I can do that carefully and explain the change. I would not call it secure work unless a clinic or firm pays for that call.

headlineQuote: A savings account is a cushion, not a payslip.
portrait: At **fifty-eight**, Wendy drafts dental-practice accounts and tax returns as a junior.
Her **accounting bachelor’s** accompanies below-average skill and continued senior sign-off.
She **never uses AI**, relying on booking records and a familiar checklist.
Ravi’s **shop wage**, grown daughters, paid-off home and eleven-month reserve give stability.
Her **higher junior pay** and many nearby firms allow a careful search if work shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her dental-account drafting wage despite household assets.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, a posted funded job and a signed start.
